newsitem.title: KENYA: South Africa, EU push for Zaire ceasefire.
newsitem.headline: South Africa, EU push for Zaire ceasefire.

text.p: African leaders gathered in Nairobi for talks on Wednesday on the Zaire crisis with Zaire's prime minister, who is under pressure from both parliament and rebel advances.
Before the start of the Nairobi meeting, South African Foreign Minister Alfred Nzo and a European envoy said they hoped for a ceasefire in Zaire to pave the way for a political settlement.
After talks with Zairean Prime Minister Kengo wa Dondo on Wednesday morning, Nzo told Reuters: "We are hopeful for a ceasefire. We have always been hopeful although it has not happened yet."
"A ceasefire in Zaire is important because it would be the foundation for any political process."
Kenyan President Daniel arap Moi was hosting Wednesday's meeting with Nzo, the presidents of Cameroon, Zimbabwe and Congo and beleaguered Kengo representing ailing Zairean President Mobutu Sese Seko.

On Tuesday, the Zairean parliament in Kinshasa in a disputed vote called for the sacking of Kengo, who backs a military solution to the rebellion in the east and has served as prime minister since 1994.
The European Union Special Envoy to the Great Lakes region of central Africa, Aldo Ajello, also held talks with Kengo and said Wednesday's meeting would seek ways to achieve a ceasefire.
He said it would also prepare an agenda for next week's extraordinary summit in Togo of the Organisation of African Unity (OAU) on the conflict in Africa's third largest country.

"A ceasefire is an important part of a political process in Zaire. We hope for a ceasefire soon and that is why this meeting in Nairobi is very important," said Ajello. "The meeting will also work out an agenda for next week's OAU summit in Lome."
Nzo and Ajello said they could not say how the meeting would address Zaire's refusal to talk to rebel leader Laurent Kabila and his vow to continue the war.

Ajello, U.N. special envoy Mohamed Sahnoun and OAU Secretary -General Salim Ahmed Salim are attending the Nairobi meeting as observers. The rebels were not invited and accuse Moi of trying to prop up Mobutu.

Supporters of Kengo and Mobutu said the vote in Kinshasa on Tuesday was flawed because too few transitional parliament members took part. But opposition militants planned to demonstrate on Wednesday in the capital in support of the vote.

Kengo's presence in Nairobi, where he arrived on Tuesday, followed a Zairean government boycott of two previous rounds of talks on Zaire in the Kenyan capital. The government had demanded the withdrawal of all foreign forces before attending.
Kinshasa accuses Rwanda, Uganda and Burundi of sending troops into eastern Zaire to fight alongside the rebels. All three countries have denied any involvement.
Kabila's Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire has seized more than a fifth of Zaire with the latest prize being Kisangani, the country's third largest city.
Diplomats, speaking before the parliamentary vote against Kengo, expected little progress in Nairobi without representatives of rebels and their allies Uganda and Rwanda.

Kenya, South Africa, Zimbabwe and Cameroon were mandated by a "Nairobi Two" summit last December to lead African efforts to end the Zaire fighting. Kabila has ruled out any ceasefire before talks with Mobutu, 66, on his stepping down.
